replacements.new: - **Shuffled labels.** The same images and captions, but labels are randomly permuted across the 200 images. Under this exchangeable-label null, image-to-text R@1 has expectation 0.10 and class-mean rows have no systematic class alignment. One finite permutation need not produce exactly flat rows or exactly 0.10; retain and compare its observed matrix and retrieval scores.

**Controls.** With the image labels shuffled, the class-mean matrix is almost the same in every row, and R@1 falls to 0.135 and 0.14 (chance is 0.10; with 200 images, differences

the 200 images belong to any one class). The noise panel isn't blank, however: it has *column* structure, meaning that some captions are more similar to every image than others.
Hold on to that caption-specific bias: it comes back, with consequences, in the binding test.

replacements.new:
**Controls.** With the image labels shuffled, the observed class-mean rows are similar and image-to-text R@1 is 0.135 and 0.14, compared with null expectation 0.10. These are finite observed deviations, not a calibrated significance test. A claim about unusually high retrieval would need a specified permutation statistic and its null distribution; no such interval or p-value is computed here. With noise images R@1 is 0.10: choosing the same caption for every image also gives 20/200 on this balanced set. The noise panel retains column structure, so some captions are more similar to every image than others. Keep that caption-specific bias in mind for the binding test.

</details>
